ideas.title: Amazon Built a $20B Chip Empire and Wall Street Is Watching the Wrong Earnings Call
ideas.trend: Amazon's Q1 2026 earnings revealed a custom chip business at a $20B annual run rate, triple-digit YoY growth, and $225B in committed Trainium orders — the largest AI chip backlog in the market.
ideas.consensus: NVIDIA dominates AI chips; the hyperscalers are building alternatives that pose a future risk.
ideas.angle: The risk already materialized. Amazon's chip backlog exceeds NVIDIA's entire annual revenue. Trainium is sold out through multiple product generations. This is a business, not a hedge — and the coverage asymmetry between NVIDIA's May 20 earnings and Amazon's Q1 disclosures tells you exactly how undercovered the shift already is.

content_pack.x_longform:
Amazon built a chip empire. The backlog is larger than NVIDIA's entire annual revenue.

NVIDIA reports on May 20. Analysts project $78.5 billion in Q1 revenue. The options market is pricing a meaningful chance Jensen Huang walks away as the head of the most valuable company on Earth. Wall Street's attention is entirely on Blackwell.

Meanwhile, Andy Jassy disclosed on the Q1 earnings call that Amazon's custom silicon division is sitting on $225 billion in committed Trainium orders. If the division were standalone, Jassy said, the run rate would be closer to $50 billion annually.

The Q1 numbers tell the rest.

Amazon's custom chip business posted triple-digit year-over-year growth. Forty percent quarter-over-quarter. Annual run rate past $20 billion, per The Register's coverage of the Q1 call. For context: AMD's entire chip business runs at roughly $25 billion a year. Intel's data center division runs at $12 billion.

The scale is worth pausing on. NVIDIA's entire annual revenue is roughly $130 billion. Amazon holds $225 billion in chip revenue commitments, for a product line most market watchers still treat as a footnote to the AWS story. The coverage asymmetry is not small.

Now the product slate. Trainium2: sold out. Price-performance 30% better than comparable NVIDIA GPUs. Trainium3: started shipping in Q1. Thirty to forty percent better than Trainium2 on price-performance. Nearly fully subscribed before broad availability. Trainium4: 18 months from shipping. Already largely reserved.

The hyperscaler-building-alternatives narrative treats this as a future risk to NVIDIA. It is a present reality.

Amazon's structural position runs differently from NVIDIA's. NVIDIA sells to five hyperscalers. Four of those five fund programs designed to replace it. Microsoft Maia. Meta MTIA. AWS Trainium. Google TPU. The biggest customers and the biggest existential threats share the same balance sheet.

Amazon's chip business sits on the other side. Its primary customer is Amazon itself. AWS grew 28% in Q1, its fastest rate in 15 quarters, and much of that compute runs on Trainium infrastructure Amazon already owns. When Trainium undercuts NVIDIA on total cost of ownership, AWS wins more cloud contracts. The chip loop feeds the cloud loop.

Google operates the same structure. SemiAnalysis pegs the seventh-generation Ironwood TPU at 44% lower total cost of ownership than NVIDIA's GB200 in a finished rack. Anthropic locked in 1 million TPUs and 5 gigawatts of capacity. Meta signed a multibillion-dollar TPU lease. Google sits on both sides of the AI compute tax.

Amazon is closing in on the same position. The $225 billion Trainium backlog means external customers are now signing multi-year commitments to chips that have not fully shipped yet. The demand has moved outside Amazon's own balance sheet.

In 2000, every dollar flowing into internet buildout had to pass through Cisco's networking gear. Cisco held the most valuable seat in the market for exactly as long as it was uncontested.

Amazon is building infrastructure that does not require an outside chip supplier if you are Amazon. The $225 billion backlog is the first concrete signal of how far beyond Amazon's own needs that demand has already spread.

The chip company hiding inside the cloud just got too big to stay hidden.

content_pack.substack_draft:
$225 billion. That is the total revenue Amazon has committed across its Trainium chip orders. Most people I talk to in tech know the hyperscalers are building GPU alternatives. Almost none know that Amazon's chip business has already crossed a $20 billion annual run rate, grew triple digits year over year, and is sold out through the next product generation.

The framing I keep seeing is that hyperscaler chip programs pose a future risk to NVIDIA. That framing is several years behind the actual data. Amazon and Google both operate chip businesses that are not substitutes in the abstract, but are already winning market share in the workloads where total cost of ownership matters most. SemiAnalysis pegs Google's Ironwood TPU at 44% lower TCO than NVIDIA's GB200 in a finished rack. Amazon's Trainium3 is 30 to 40% better on price-performance than its predecessor and is nearly fully subscribed before broad availability.

I am not sure what this means for NVIDIA's May 20 earnings. The Blackwell backlog looks real. The pricing power looks intact. But the $225 billion in committed Trainium orders is also real, and it is structural, not speculative. Revenue commitments are harder to reverse than press releases about chip alternatives.

The question I keep returning to: at what point does the hyperscaler chip business get treated as an independent competitive force rather than a footnote to the AWS earnings story? The $225 billion number suggests we may already be past that inflection point.

ideas.title: Perplexity Bet $400M on Distribution. It Was the Wrong Bet.
ideas.trend: Snap disclosed in Q1 2026 earnings that its $400M AI search integration deal with Perplexity 'amicably ended' after six months of testing without ever reaching a broad rollout.
ideas.consensus: The deal failed due to a product mismatch — Perplexity's AI search was not the right fit for Snapchat's interface.
ideas.angle: AI consumer products win by replacing a habit, not by embedding inside someone else's. Snapchat users open Snapchat for Snapchat. No distribution capital buys a different user intent.

content_pack.x_longform:
Every AI company has the same distribution thesis: get inside the apps people already use. Perplexity tested it with Snapchat. Fourteen months, $400 million committed, and a Q1 earnings disclosure that the relationship "amicably ended," per TechCrunch.

Snapchat has 450 million daily users. None of them had to change their relationship with Snapchat for the AI search integration to work. That was the entire problem.

Consumer AI scales by becoming the destination. Being a feature inside someone else's app leaves the product hostage to someone else's users' habits.
content_pack.x_thread:
Tweet 1: Every AI company has the same distribution thesis: get inside the apps people already use. Perplexity just ran the $400M test. Result: "amicably ended."

Tweet 2: The deal, announced last November: Perplexity would pay Snap $400M in cash and equity over a year to integrate AI search inside Snapchat's Chat interface. Dead by Q1, per TechCrunch.

Tweet 3: Snapchat has 450M daily users. None of them had to change their habit for the integration to work. They open Snapchat to see friends, not to ask AI questions. The intent layer is entirely different.

Tweet 4: This is the first large-scale public test of "embed AI into existing apps" theory. The stated reason: "not the right fit." The simpler reason: you cannot borrow user intent.

Tweet 5: Perplexity's distribution strategy depends on platform deals. This was the flagship one. The $400M evaporated before a broad rollout. Consumer AI scales by becoming the destination, not a feature inside someone else's app.

Tweet 6: The only AI products with durable consumer distribution built their own habits. ChatGPT. Claude. Gemini. None of them won by embedding inside a platform they don't control.
content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people, including me, assumed the Snap and Perplexity deal would at least reach a full rollout before it collapsed. The logic seemed sound: Perplexity gets exposure to 450 million daily Snapchat users, Snap gets $400 million and an AI story to tell investors. Both sides had clear incentives to make it work.

The more I sit with why it failed, the less I think it was a product execution problem. The stated reason is that the integration was "not the right fit for each company's product goals." The simpler version: Snapchat users open Snapchat to see photos and videos from friends. The intent behind that action is entirely different from the intent behind asking an AI a question. You cannot retrofit a search behavior onto a social feed.

This matters beyond Snap. There is a whole theory of AI consumer distribution that says you win by getting inside the platforms people already use. The assumption is that AI is a feature that sits inside existing behavior. The Snap result is the most concrete public test of that assumption I have seen, and it did not hold.

I do not know yet whether this is a verdict on platform distribution as a strategy in general, or just on Perplexity's specific implementation. But I find myself more skeptical of the "borrow someone else's users" model than I was six months ago. The AI products with the most durable consumer adoption seem to have built their own habit loops rather than borrowed them.

ideas.title: FIS Just Closed Its TSYS Deal. The $40B Reshuffling of Payment Rails Is Done.
ideas.trend: FIS completed its $13.5B acquisition of Global Payments' Issuer Solutions (TSYS) in May 2026, finalizing the biggest restructuring of legacy payment rail infrastructure since 2019 — with Worldpay changing hands three times over the same period.
ideas.consensus: Legacy payment processors are consolidating through specialization — FIS focuses on card issuing, Global Payments on merchant acquiring — to compete more effectively.
ideas.angle: Both companies just doubled down on their lane while shedding what does not fit. Specialization defers the fundamental question — what payment rails are worth when a cheaper parallel set is being built on stablecoins — it does not answer it. Three Worldpay owners in six years is the market asking that question out loud.

content_pack.x_longform:
Worldpay has had three owners since 2019. That is not a payments M&A story. It is a payments strategy crisis.

FIS bought Worldpay outright in 2019. GTCR took a controlling stake in 2023. Global Payments completed the full acquisition in January for $24.25 billion, per its own press release. FIS just completed the other side of the transaction: a $13.5 billion acquisition of Global Payments' Issuer Solutions business, formerly TSYS. The full $40 billion reshuffling is now done.

The industry is repricing faster than the incumbents can answer the fundamental question: what are payment rails worth when a parallel set can be built on stablecoins at a fraction of the cost?

Here is what is happening structurally. FIS traded away Worldpay, the world's largest merchant acquirer, to get TSYS, one of the largest card issuing processors. Global Payments traded TSYS to get Worldpay. Each company doubled down on its lane. Both companies got bigger. The fundamental pressure on legacy payment infrastructure did not get smaller.

Payment processors earn from infrastructure designed in the 1970s. ACH, card networks, correspondent banking. The rails sit underneath every transaction in global commerce, invisible and rent-generating. That model compounds well when nothing challenges the rails.

Stablecoin legislation is in final Senate negotiation. Seven major economies, including the UAE, EU, and Singapore, now mandate reserve backing and licensed issuers for stablecoins. Settlement is happening on-chain at a fraction of traditional card costs. The parallel rails are being built in parallel with the $40 billion consolidation.

The Worldpay cash flows are real. Merchant relationships are sticky. The $24 billion price tag is not irrational on its own terms.

But three owners in six years means each acquirer eventually confronts the same constraint: the business earns its returns from infrastructure its customers would replace if they could.

Three owners in six years is the market asking that question. Not answering it.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people are reading the FIS-TSYS deal as a payments consolidation story. Each company doubles down on its specialty, the industry gets more efficient, standard M&A logic. I think it is a different story.

Worldpay has had three distinct owners since 2019. FIS bought it outright, then sold a controlling stake to GTCR in 2023, then Global Payments acquired the whole thing in January for $24.25 billion. FIS, in turn, just completed its $13.5 billion acquisition of Global Payments' TSYS business. The full reshuffling is now done. Forty billion dollars moved to reorganize the legacy payment stack into two camps: an issuer-focused FIS and a merchant-acquirer-focused Global Payments.

The timing is worth noting. Stablecoin legislation is in final Senate negotiation. Seven major economies now have regulatory frameworks mandating reserve backing and licensed issuers. Settlement is happening on-chain at a fraction of traditional card rail costs. The parallel infrastructure is being built at the same time as the $40 billion consolidation.

I am not arguing Global Payments made a bad bet. The Worldpay cash flows are real. Merchant relationships are among the stickiest in finance. But I keep asking why no single acquirer has held Worldpay for more than four years, and the answer I come back to is that each one eventually realizes the business earns its returns from infrastructure their customers would replace if they could afford to.

Whether stablecoins actually reach the scale to challenge card rails is still genuinely uncertain. But three owners in six years is not just M&A activity. It is the market trying to figure out where this asset belongs in a world where the rails underneath it are being contested.
